idiom_name: struct { From time.Time; Until *time.Time } + EffectiveOn(asOf time.Time) bool
implementation_notes: Go has no date-only type: time.Time is an instant carrying a Location and, for values that came from time.Now(), a monotonic clock reading that governs Before/After/Compare/Sub - so a date-granularity period must never be built from time.Now(). Construct bounds with time.Date(y, m, d, 0, 0, 0, 0, time.UTC) (or time.Parse("2006-01-02", s), which yields UTC) and store a *time.Time for the open end; strip a monotonic reading with t.Round(0) if a wall-clock value ever reaches the comparison. The rickb777/date variant replaces this with a genuine civil-date type when dates rather than instants are the domain; instant-based time.Time ranges remain the right choice for timestamp-granularity validity such as leases or sessions.
pitfalls: Values from time.Now() carry a monotonic reading that Before/After/Compare use and that the == operator includes; mixing them with parsed dates makes comparisons ignore the wall clock - strip it with t.Round(0) or build every bound explicitly.

The Location is part of the value: a date parsed in Local and one stored in UTC can be a day apart for the same calendar date, and time.Time must not be used as a map or database key without normalising both.
AddDate interprets months and days in the value's Location, so "plus one month" across a DST transition is not a fixed number of hours - calendar arithmetic belongs to the date type, not the instant.

variants.name: rickb777/date civil dates (optional dependency, v2)
variants.implementation_notes: The date module supplies what the standard library lacks: a storage-efficient civil-date type (an integer day count, so ordering uses Go's own operators, with years outside 0-9999 representable) plus a timespan.DateRange type that expresses a period between two dates. Use it when validity periods are date-granularity - tariffs, contracts, assignments - and a dependency is acceptable; the stdlib variant stays the choice when the period must align to instants or no third-party module may be added. The period struct in the domain remains your own type either way, because the library models dates and periods, not the write-side non-overlap rule.
variants.idiom_name: github.com/rickb777/date/v2 date.Date bounds + the module's timespan.DateRange
pitfalls: date.Date's zero value is year 0, not an unset date in the common era: a zeroed bound silently means "always" or "never" depending on the comparison - use a documented sentinel or a pointer.
v1 stored days since 1970 and v2 since year zero: integers persisted by v1 code must be migrated (the module documents adding date.ZeroOffset) or every stored bound shifts by about 1970 years.
Mixing date.Date and time.Time in one model reintroduces the Location problem; convert at the boundary once and keep the domain in civil dates.
